verses.text: After this David asked the LORD, “Should I go up to one of Judah's towns?” The LORD said, “Go up.” David asked where, and the LORD said, “To Hebron.”
So David went up with his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal from Carmel.
He brought his men and their households too. They settled in the towns around Hebron.
The men of Judah came and anointed David king over Judah. They told him, “The men of Jabesh Gilead buried Saul.”
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead and said, “May the LORD bless you for showing this kindness to Saul, your lord, by burying him.
May the LORD show you faithful love and loyalty. I'll also repay you for the kindness you've shown.
Now be strong and brave. Saul your lord is dead, and the people of Judah have anointed me king over them.”
Meanwhile Abner son of Ner, Saul's army commander, took Saul's son Ishbosheth to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Saul's son Ishbosheth was forty when he became king over Israel. He reigned two years, while Judah followed David.
David reigned over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the men of Saul's son Ishbosheth went from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David's men met them at the pool of Gibeon. The two groups sat on opposite sides of the pool.
Abner told Joab, “Let's have the young men get up and compete in front of us.” Joab answered, “Let them get up.”
Twelve men stepped forward for Benjamin and Saul's son Ishbosheth, and twelve stepped forward for David.
Each grabbed his opponent by the head and drove his sword into the other's side. They all fell together, so that place at Gibeon was called Helkath Hazzurim.
The battle was fierce that day. David's men defeated Abner and the army of Israel.
Zeruiah's three sons were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel could run as fast as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased Abner, refusing to turn aside to the right or left.
Abner looked back and asked, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.”
Abner told him, “Turn aside and take the armor of one of the young men.” But Asahel refused to stop chasing him.
Abner told him again, “Stop following me. Why should I strike you down? How could I face your brother Joab afterward?”
Asahel still refused. Abner struck him with the back end of his spear, and Asahel died where he fell. Everyone who came to that spot stopped.
Joab and Abishai kept chasing Abner. The sun went down as they reached the hill of Ammah opposite Giah, on the road toward the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites rallied behind Abner and stood together on a hilltop.
Abner called to Joab, “Will the sword keep devouring forever? Don't you see how bitter this will end? How long will you wait before telling your men to stop chasing their own brothers?”
Joab said, “As surely as God lives, if you hadn't spoken, my men would have kept chasing their brothers until morning.”
Joab blew the trumpet, and everyone stopped. They gave up the chase and stopped fighting Israel.
Abner and his men marched through the Arabah all night, crossed the Jordan, went through all of Bithron, and reached Mahanaim.
Joab came back from chasing Abner and gathered his men. Nineteen of David's men were missing, besides Asahel.
David's men had killed three hundred sixty of the Benjaminites and Abner's men.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men traveled through the night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
